claims.claim: Islam emerged in Arabia in the seventh century CE; Muslims regard Muhammad (c. 570-632 CE), a Meccan who worked in the caravan trade, as a prophet and messenger of God, not a divine being, and as the final prophet in a line that includes figures such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus.

The traditional founding event of the Muslim community is the hijra: in 622 CE Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, and Muslims for practical purposes date their religion from that migration.

Muslims describe the Quran as the revealed scripture: the word of God delivered to Muhammad by the archangel Gabriel, divided into 114 suras (chapters), and regarded as the fundamental source of Islamic teaching.

The six articles of faith, named descriptively as introductory accounts present them: tawhid (the oneness of God), belief in angels, revealed scriptures, prophets, the Day of Judgment, and divine decree (also translated as predestination).

The Five Pillars are commonly described as shahada (the profession of faith), salat (ritual prayers performed five times each day), zakat (alms or charity to benefit the poor and needy), sawm (fasting during the month of Ramadan), and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).

The Hadith are compilations of sayings and deeds attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, providing written documentation of his words and example (the Sunnah); different communities hold different collections authoritative — six collections for Sunnis and four for the Shia, as Britannica describes.

The division between Sunni and Shia Muslims began early in Islam's history as a question of who should lead the community after Muhammad's death; the Shia trace to a faction known as the 'party of Ali' that supported Ali ibn Abi Talib, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet and later fourth caliph, and his descendants, while the Sunnis became the majority branch.

Sufism is a mystical tradition within Islam in which practitioners seek the truth of divine love and knowledge through direct personal experience of God, typically along spiritual paths; Sufis have played a significant role in Muslim societies.

Islam is a global religion: the second-largest religion in the world, with more than 1.5 billion adherents by the early 21st century; Indonesia has the largest Muslim population, and Muslims span the globe, with Islam present across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas.

Daily life in Muslim communities commonly includes five daily ritual prayers (often at the mosque, where Friday congregational prayer includes a sermon), dietary rules that distinguish permitted (halal) from forbidden foods with pork and alcohol traditionally forbidden, and two major festivals: Eid al-Fitr, marking the end of the Ramadan fast, and Eid al-Adha, the festival of sacrifice that coincides with the culmination of the hajj pilgrimage.
The mosque is the Muslim place of worship and, beyond prayer, an important social center of the Muslim community.
Introductory accounts describe the Kaaba, the cube-shaped sanctuary in Mecca, as the most sacred site in Islam, toward which Muslims face in prayer and to which the hajj pilgrimage is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the Arabic word 'Islam' is translated
positions: Britannica: islām literally means 'surrender' — the believer accepts surrender to the will of God.
BBC Religions: 'The word Islam means submission to the will of God.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says the word is often translated as submission or surrender to God, and notes that some glosses connect it to the Arabic word for peace; no single translation is presented as the only one.

positions: Britannica (early 21st century): 'more than 1.5 billion Muslims worldwide'.
OpenStax: 'about one-fifth of the world's population identifies as Muslim.'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses Britannica's more recent figure (more than 1.5 billion) and the agreement across sources that Islam is the second-largest religion; the older BBC figure is not used.

positions: OpenStax states 'born in Mecca... in 570 C.E.' as a plain date.
Wikipedia and Britannica present the date as approximate (c. 570).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson writes c. 570-632 CE to signal that the early dates are approximate, following the cautious phrasing.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's claim that Islam is 'a foundational concept in Religious Studies' is boilerplate, not a claim about the tradition, and was discarded.

The generated draft's definition of Islam as 'a label on a toolbox drawer' and its framing of the topic as a generic concept to 'define, recognize, and apply' were unsupported editorial filler and were replaced with descriptive content.
The generated draft contained no factual claims about Islam's origins, beliefs, practices, or texts; all lesson content was researched and written from sources.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate (which described no actual content of Islam) with a fully sourced, descriptive lesson.
Dated the hijra to 622 CE and described it as the traditional founding event, per Britannica and BBC Religions.
Described the Quran in general terms and never quoted it, per project policy.
Presented the Sunni-Shia division as an early historical dispute over leadership after Muhammad's death, described factually, per Britannica and the Pluralism Project.
Softened the translation of 'Islam' to 'submission or surrender to God' with a note on the 'peace' gloss, per the conflicting-evidence resolution.
Used approximate dating (c. 570-632 CE) for Muhammad rather than a bare 570 C.E.

sourceRecords.title: 15.2 World Religions — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: Islam as monotheistic, following the teaching of the prophet Muhammad, born in Mecca in 570 C.E.; Muhammad seen as prophet and messenger, not divine; followers called Muslims; Islam glossed as 'peace' and 'submission'; the Qur'an as the sacred text; the five pillars (one God and Muhammad his prophet, daily prayer, helping the poor, fasting, pilgrimage to Mecca); about one-fifth of the world identifying as Muslim; Indonesia as the country with the most Muslims; Muslims spanning the globe; Muslims as the third-largest U.S. religious group; the Kaaba in Mecca as the most sacred place for Muslim practice.

sourceRecords.title: Religions: Islam (with 'Islam at a glance' and 'Five Pillars of Islam')
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21: the landing page, https://www.bbc.co.uk/religion/religions/islam/ataglance/glance.shtml, and https://www.bbc.co.uk/religion/religions/islam/practices/fivepillars.shtml (BBC's archived pages are still served). Supports: the word Islam meaning 'submission to the will of God'; Islam as the second-largest religion with over 1 billion followers; belief in one God (Allah); God sending a number of prophets, with Jesus, Moses, and Abraham respected as prophets and Muhammad as the final Prophet; Muslims dating their religion from the migration of Muhammad; the Qur'an and the Sunnah (the practical example of the Prophet) as the bases of law; the Five Pillars with one-line descriptions (Shahadah: sincerely reciting the profession of faith; Salat: ritual prayers in the proper way five times each day; Zakat: alms/charity tax to benefit the poor and needy; Sawm: fasting during Ramadan; Hajj: pilgrimage to Mecca); and the site's listing of Sufism, Sunni and Shi'a, and the holy days Eid ul Fitr and Eid ul Adha.

sourceRecords.title: Islam (religion)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive captures (2018 snapshot and 2024 snapshot of britannica.com/topic/Islam) because britannica.com blocks automated fetching; the copies read are recorded here. Supports: Islam promulgated by the Prophet Muhammad in Arabia in the 7th century CE; islām literally 'surrender', the believer accepts surrender to the will of Allah; Allah as sole God; in 622 CE the Prophet migrated to Medina and the community-state of Islam emerged; the Qur'an regarded as the verbatim word of God delivered to Muhammad by the archangel Gabriel, divided into 114 suras, the fundamental source of Islamic teaching; Muhammad as the last of a series of prophets (Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Solomon, Jesus); the shahadah as the first pillar (profession of faith) with derived beliefs in (1) angels (particularly Gabriel), (2) the revealed Book (the Qur'an and the sacred books of Judaism and Christianity), (3) a series of prophets, and (4) the Last Day (Day of Judgment); five daily canonical prayers, the mosque, muezzin, imam, and facing Mecca; zakat as an annual payment used primarily for the poor (2.5 percent on cash and precious metals); the Last Day, resurrection, and judgment according to deeds; Hadith as compilations of sayings attributed to the Prophet ('report'), with six collections especially authoritative for Sunnis and four for the Shi'ah; more than 1.5 billion Muslims worldwide in the early 21st century; Islam as the second most practiced religion globally; consumption of alcohol and pork forbidden in Islamic tradition; Friday congregational prayers with a sermon; the Ka'bah sanctuary in Mecca; and the festival of sacrifice (Eid al-Adha) connected to the hajj.

sourceRecords.title: Tawhid
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2026-08-01) because britannica.com blocks automated fetching. Supports: tawhid ('making one', 'asserting oneness') as, in Islam, the oneness of God — that God is one and there is no god but he, as stated in the shahadah formula; God as a unity, not composed of parts.

sourceRecords.title: Sufism
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2026-08-10) because britannica.com blocks automated fetching. Supports: Sufism as a mystical Islamic belief and practice in which Muslims seek the truth of divine love and knowledge through direct personal experience of God; Sufism consisting of mystical paths; its growth from early Islamic asceticism; and the significant role of Sufis in forming Muslim society.

sourceRecords.title: Eid al-Fitr
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2024 snapshot) because britannica.com blocks automated fetching. Supports: Eid al-Fitr as the first of the two canonical festivals of Islam; it marks the end of Ramadan, the Muslim holy month of fasting; it is distinguished by communal prayer at daybreak; it is a time of visits, gifts, and new clothes.

sourceRecords.title: Eid al-Adha
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2026-08-13) because britannica.com blocks automated fetching. Supports: Eid al-Adha ('Festival of Sacrifice') as one of the two major festivals in Islam, marking the culmination of the hajj pilgrimage; it commemorates Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son Ishmael as an act of obedience to God; celebrated by Muslims throughout the world with communal prayer and, for families that can afford it, animal sacrifice with meat shared.

sourceRecords.title: Shi'ite
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read via Internet Archive capture (2019-07-16) because britannica.com blocks automated fetching. Supports: the Shi'ite as a member of the smaller of the two major branches of Islam, distinguished from the majority Sunnis; early in the history of Islam the Shi'ites were a political faction (Arabic shi'at 'Ali, 'party of Ali') supporting the power of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth caliph and successor of Muhammad, and later his descendants; this faction gradually developed into a religious movement, Shi'ism.

sourceRecords.title: Islam (resources on Islamic traditions)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. pluralism.org blocks automated fetching (Akamai); read via Internet Archive capture (2016-03-21) of the Pluralism Project's Islam resource directory. Supports: the Pluralism Project's framing of Islam through sections titled 'Qur'an: The Word of God', 'Muhammad: The Messenger of God', 'One Ummah with Many Views', 'Sunni and Shi'i Interpretations', 'Sufism: Seeking God', 'The Five Pillars', and 'Islam in America'; the shahadah as one of the Five Pillars that defines the foundations of Muslim life; and the conviction, as the page puts it, that God is one and has sent messengers to guide humanity.

sourceRecords.title: Islam (encyclopedia article)
sourceRecords.notes: Supporting source. Read live on 2026-08-21 via the wikitext endpoint (en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Islam&action=raw) to avoid page-weight. Supports: the Islamic creed requiring belief in six articles — God, angels, revelation, prophets, the Day of Resurrection, and divine predestination; tawhid as the oneness of God and a precise monotheism; the mosque as the place of worship for Muslims whose primary purpose is prayer but which is also an important social centre for the Muslim community; and the Five Pillars as shahada, salah, zakat, sawm (fasting in Ramadan), and hajj.
